articles.title: Red Roses: England's Delaney Burns on key opportunity to progress international career
articles.summary: As Delaney Burns hopes to be selected to face Australia, she talks to BBC Sport about another opportunity to add to her six caps in a so-far whirlwind career.
articles.body:
Delaney Burns revealed to her England team-mates that at 15 years old she had a 'short back and sides' - it went down well.

Having been selected to speak at one of the Red Roses 'connection meetings', the 24-year-old admitted she had "never been so nervous to talk in front of a group of people" in her life.

But the second-row was a roaring success as she covered her rugby journey, life in Bristol and 'that' haircut.

As she prepares to face Australia this Saturday, she has another opportunity to add to her six caps in what has been a whirlwind career so far.

Still only 24, Burns won her first three caps for England in 2023, then had to patiently wait for a call-up into the 2026 Six Nations squad to add three more.

With Abbie Ward, Rosie Galligan and Zoe Stratford all away from the squad pregnant or on maternity leave, the upcoming WXV Global Series is a significant opportunity for Burns.

"This is the first kind of campaign that I've been brought in from the start," she says.

"Being deemed as a more experienced forward, especially around the line-out, is something I want to hold myself quite high to and we do have a few younger players in the squad now, a few people coming through. So, I'm just trying to be a bit more of a person of knowledge to look to and help them out and build on my own strength."

Having missed out on one of England's 32-contracted places , she's focusing on her defence this season and wants to reach the next level.

As Burns continues to find her feet in the squad, an area she's excelled in off-field has been her work with the Bristol Bears Foundation. She coaches and gives talks to girls at schools in the greater Bristol area, covering more than just rugby.

"We talk about the menstrual cycle and how it affects you," she says. "Rugby is a really good sport to help with the idea of body image.

"We look at the effects that social media has in terms of too much screen time and filtering and AI. How to stay mentally safe as well as physically safe.

"There's some really deprived areas of Bristol - our whole mantra is to take those areas and do what we can to give the kids in those communities an opportunity, which I find very rewarding."

The impact of the work she's done with the foundation has seen the launch of a South Bristol girls team that's attracted 50-60 players and counting.

As she seeks a seventh cap against Australia on Saturday, will she take any of her own advice?

"I should listen to my own voice a bit more, probably," she says. "There are times where I definitely find myself in a bit of a weird headspace, camp is always hard.

"It's really rewarding and it's an exciting place to be and I wouldn't change it for the world, but equally it can be quite difficult. So yeah, listening to my own advice probably would be quite beneficial."

One of Burns' greatest fans is her grandad. If selected on Saturday, he'll be making the trip up to Manchester from Poole.

"He got me into rugby, trained me and goes to all the games he can," she says.

The stories about old hairstyles may have raised a few smiles among team-mates, but Burns is taking a more serious approach to the season ahead.

If selected against Australia, she will have another opportunity to add to her international experience and strengthen her place in an increasingly competitive Red Roses squad, with one of her biggest supporters watching on from the stands.

articles.title: Rob Baxter: Exeter boss says England should pick English-based players
articles.summary: Exeter director of rugby Rob Baxter says England's rules on selecting only home-based players are the right thing for the domestic game.
articles.body:
Exeter director of rugby Rob Baxter says England's rules on selecting only home-based players are the right thing for the domestic game.

Former England forward Courtney Lawes has called for overseas-based players to be eligible to be picked for the England side.

The 37-year-old, who has won 105 England caps, returned to the Prem this summer with Sale, having spent two years at French side Brive where he was ineligible to represent his country.

Under England's selection policy, players can only be called up from overseas clubs in exceptional circumstances.

Baxter feels it is important the rules are not changed.

"I just don't think, for the good of the English game, you can do it," he told BBC Sport. "It's not that I don't understand the arguments, I do.

Allow overseas stars to play for England - Lawes

"There's two arguments here, do you just want to make all the best players available to play for England or do you want to build Premiership Rugby as part of how you build the England team?

"If the two go together then you have to have some kind of rules and regulations around where the English players play.

"I always caveat any argument and say selfishly I'm talking about what's good for Exeter Chiefs as well - because what's good for Exeter, and every other Premiership side, is knowing there's a real reason for your best English players to stay in this country.

"If it just comes down to purely finance, then it's a tough, competitive situation for us, and when people just throw it out there that players should be allowed to play anywhere they like, I think you've got to look down at the deeper repercussions of what may actually happen in the English game overall."

Under the rules as they stand, England are unable to call on players such as Toulouse back row Jack Willis - who was voted the best player in France in 2024-25 - as well as Kyle Sinckler, Manu Tuilagi, Billy Vunipola, Lewis Ludlam and former Exeter star Sam Simmonds.

Prem clubs benefit from central payments from the Rugby Football Union (RFU) for their England players, with the national side having a greater say on their management as a result.

England's policy is similar to that of Ireland and New Zealand, while nations such as Scotland, South Africa and Australia do pick players from overseas.

"You can't pick and choose a model just to decide this is what will be good or bad for a country," added Baxter.

"For some countries they're very strict on it and it works really well for them. We've got to decide what we're comfortable with and stick to it."
